DRC Imposes Tariffs on Imported Oil & Gas Services Equipment, Industry Faces Immediate Cost Pressures

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has implemented a new tariff regime on imported Oil & Gas Services & Equipment, effective June 10, raising import duties by 25% on drilling rigs, wellhead systems, and related equipment. The government stated the measure aims to encourage local development of technical capacities, but industry participants warn of significant cost implications for ongoing operations.

According to the Congolese Oilfield Services Association, at least nine major service firms are currently affected, including Kinshasa Drilling Partners and Lubumbashi Well Solutions. “Our projected operating expenses have risen sharply overnight,” said Pascal Mbuyi, operations manager at Kinshasa Drilling Partners. “Several of our rigs are due for replacement parts that must now clear customs at the new rates, putting immediate strain on our budgets.”

Industry analysts estimate that the tariffs could raise project costs by an average of 12-18% for firms dependent on imported equipment. The increased expenses are already prompting some companies to reconsider capital investments and delay scheduled site expansions. At least four field sites in the Haut-Katanga and Tshopo provinces have reported postponements of maintenance activities.

Union representatives have expressed concern for local workers. “We fear that increased operating costs may lead to job cuts or reduced hours,” said David Kalombo of the DRC Oil & Gas Services Workers Union. With roughly 8,000 workers employed in the sector nationwide, uncertainty about future staffing levels is rising.

The DRC’s Ministry of Trade said in a statement that it will review the tariff’s impact quarterly. In the meantime, industry leaders are urging the government to consider targeted exemptions for essential equipment to mitigate disruption to field operations and workforce stability. The trade-policy measure remains in effect as of publication.
